questions.question: In a patient with suspected critical illness myopathy (CIM), the muscle biopsy:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Is needed to establish the diagnosis

statements.label: B
statements.text: Is performed to define the severity of muscle injury

statements.label: C
statements.text: May show various histopathological pictures with different prognoses

statements.label: D
statements.text: Often shows myofiber necrosis

questions.explanation: [UNCONFIRMED] The source screenshot's answer-key indicators for this item were internally inconsistent with its own written feedback. Resolved here in favour of the written feedback, per this bank's standing rule that ESICM's written feedback text wins when it conflicts with the screenshot's answer markers. In selected cases of severe or persisting weakness, muscle biopsy may help define the prognosis - not establish the initial diagnosis, which (per a later item in this same assessment) is made on voluntary-contraction EMG - by showing different histopathological features such as loss of myosin (thick) filaments, fibre atrophy and necrosis. Muscle necrosis is common (reported in up to 40% of cases) and portends a worse prognosis than a thick-filament myopathy pattern. Verify against the original ESICM material if possible.
questions.topic: muscle biopsy in critical illness myopathy

questions.question: The diagnosis Guillain-Barré Syndrome:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Requires a lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) assessment performed as soon as possible

statements.label: B
statements.text: Is clinical

statements.label: C
statements.text: Nerve conduction studies support the diagnosis

statements.label: D
statements.text: Nerve conduction studies help to define the prognosis

questions.explanation: Guillain-Barré syndrome is a clinically diagnosed neurological disorder. CSF examination may show the classical cyto-albuminological dissociation - a normal cell count with an increased protein level - but this can be normal in the first week of disease, so diagnostic lumbar puncture is best performed after the first week unless bacterial or viral meningitis is suspected. Nerve conduction studies can help support the diagnosis, discriminate between axonal and demyelinating forms, and relate to prognosis, though they too can be normal early in the disease.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the Medical Research Council Sum Score?

statements.label: A
statements.text: The maximum possible score is 100

statements.label: B
statements.text: A score of less than 48% diagnoses ICU-acquired weakness

statements.label: C
statements.text: 30-40% of patients are unable to reliably perform the required tests.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Four limbs are tested, with 25 point awarded per limb

questions.explanation: The score is the sum of the scores of 6 muscle groups (3 upper-limb and 3 lower-limb) tested on each side, with a maximum score of 5 for each muscle group. The maximum overall score is therefore 60, not 100, and a score below 48 (an absolute score, not a percentage) defines ICU-acquired weakness. A substantial minority of patients (30-40%) are unable to reliably perform the required voluntary tests.
questions.topic: Medical Research Council Sum Score for ICU-acquired weakness

questions.question: Antibody tests can help the diagnosis of the cause of weakness. Which of the following is correctly matched?

statements.label: A
statements.text: Anti- acetylcholine receptor antibodies and Guillain-Barré Syndrome

statements.label: B
statements.text: Anti-MUSK antibodies and Polymyositis

statements.label: C
statements.text: Anti-synthetase antibodies and Guillain-Barré Syndrome.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Anti-MUSK antibodies and Myasthenia Gravis

questions.explanation: Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies or anti-MUSK antibodies may be present in myasthenia gravis, while anti-synthetase antibodies are associated with polymyositis, not Guillain-Barré syndrome.

questions.question: The following may hamper the clinical assessment of weakness

statements.label: A
statements.text: Neuromuscular blockade or motor blocks from regional anaesthesia

statements.label: B
statements.text: Peripheral neuropathy

statements.label: C
statements.text: Confusion or lowered Glasgow Coma Scale score

statements.label: D
statements.text: Pain

questions.explanation: Residual neuromuscular blockade decreases strength and can itself be harmful; patients receiving spinal or epidural anaesthesia/analgesia may have sensory and motor blockade for hours after the block has apparently worn off, which is important to consider in anyone who has had general or regional anaesthesia. Patients with delirium, confusion, agitation or a decrease in Glasgow Coma Scale score may not cooperate, making their assessment unreliable, and pain may limit patients' ability to move a body part, so it is important to rule out pain as a component of apparent weakness or difficulty mobilising. Peripheral neuropathy is itself a possible cause of weakness, not a factor that prevents its assessment.

questions.question: Which of the following suggest a condition of severely decreased ventilatory muscle function:

statements.label: A
statements.text: A fall in Forced Vital Capacity when assuming the supine position from the seated or standing one

statements.label: B
statements.text: An Forced Vital Capacity of less than 1 L

statements.label: C
statements.text: A decline in Forced Vital Capacity of more than 50% from baseline value.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A peak expiratory flow rate of less than 20%.

questions.explanation: Peak expiratory flow is not a test of muscle strength, so it does not indicate ventilatory muscle function; it mainly reflects large-airway calibre. A postural fall in FVC on lying supine, an absolute FVC below 1 L, and a substantial (>50%) decline from baseline are all recognised markers of severely compromised ventilatory muscle function.
questions.topic: markers of severe ventilatory muscle weakness

questions.question: In patients with neuromuscular disorders, strength testing might have to be performed at different times because:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Myasthenic symptoms may be worse at the start of the day

statements.label: B
statements.text: Some patients may be more alert and cooperative at different times

statements.label: C
statements.text: The symptoms of Guillain-Barré Syndrome are often better later in the day

statements.label: D
statements.text: Weakness from Guillain-Barré Syndrome may advance very rapidly

questions.explanation: Myasthenic symptoms are usually worse at the end of the day (fatigability with use), not the start. The weakness of Guillain-Barré syndrome does not fluctuate through the day, so it is not typically better later in the day, but it can advance very rapidly over hours to days, which is itself a reason repeat testing at different times may be needed. Patients' alertness and cooperation can also vary over the course of a day, affecting the reliability of any single test.
questions.topic: timing of strength testing in neuromuscular disorders

questions.question: In neurophysiological testing:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reduced compound muscle action potential suggests axonal neuropathy

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reduced sensory nerve action potential suggests axonal neuropathy

statements.label: C
statements.text: A 5% decrement with repetitive stimulation suggests neuromuscular failure due to persistence of neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBAs) or myasthenia gravis.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Increase in duration of compound muscle action potential suggests axonal neuropathy

questions.explanation: A reduced compound muscle action potential or a reduced sensory nerve action potential both suggest an axonal neuropathy. An increase in the duration of the compound muscle action potential is instead a feature suggestive of myopathy, not axonal neuropathy. The correct decrement threshold on repetitive stimulation is 10%, not 5%: a 10% decrement suggests neuromuscular transmission failure due to persistence of neuromuscular blocking agents or myasthenia gravis.

questions.question: Please classify each following statement as True or False:

statements.label: A
statements.text: The diaphragm is supplied by motor nerve roots C3, C4 and C5

statements.label: B
statements.text: The intercostal muscles are supplied by the long thoracic nerve of Bell (C5-C6-C7)

statements.label: C
statements.text: The accessory expiratory muscles of ventilation include sternocleidomastoid, scalene muscle, pectoral muscles, serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The accessory inspiratory muscles of ventilation include rectus abdominis, external and internal obliques and transversus abdominis.

questions.explanation: The diaphragm is supplied by motor roots C3, C4 and C5 ('C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive'). The intercostal muscles are supplied segmentally by T1-T12, not by the long thoracic nerve, which instead supplies serratus anterior (a lesion of it causes scapular winging). The muscles listed here as 'accessory expiratory' (sternocleidomastoid, scalene, pectoral muscles, serratus anterior, latissimus dorsi) are in fact accessory inspiratory muscles, while the muscles listed here as 'accessory inspiratory' (rectus abdominis, external and internal obliques, transversus abdominis) are in fact accessory expiratory muscles. The accessory expiratory muscles also include serratus posterior inferior, the lowest fibres of iliocostalis and longissimus, and quadratus lumborum.
questions.topic: innervation and accessory muscles of ventilation

questions.question: Imminent ventilator failure is suggested by:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Forced Vital Capacity of less than 40 mL/kg

statements.label: B
statements.text: Maximum Inspiratory Pressure (MIP) higher than 30 cmH2O

statements.label: C
statements.text: Maximum Expiratory pressure (MEP) lower than 40 cmH2O

statements.label: D
statements.text: Increase in duration of compound muscle action potential suggests axonal neuropathy

questions.explanation: [UNCONFIRMED] One of the four statements in this item (concerning compound muscle action potential duration and axonal neuropathy) is a neurophysiology statement unrelated in content to the question stem on imminent ventilatory failure, and appears to be a mismatched item carried over from elsewhere in the source assessment; it is transcribed verbatim with the source's marked key, but its correctness in this context should be treated with caution. For the ventilatory-failure content itself: an FVC below roughly 15-20 mL/kg (not below 40 mL/kg) and a Maximum Inspiratory Pressure lower than (not higher than) 30 cmH2O are the findings suggestive of imminent ventilatory failure.

questions.question: Electromyography diagnosis of critical illness myopathy (CIM) requires that:

statements.label: A
statements.text: The patient is awake and collaborative

statements.label: B
statements.text: Serum CK levels are abnormal

statements.label: C
statements.text: Serum myoglobin levels abnormal

statements.label: D
statements.text: Motor unit potentials are of low amplitude, short-duration and polyphasic after muscle contraction

questions.explanation: If the patient can voluntarily contract their muscle during EMG examination, CIM is revealed by motor unit potentials that are of low amplitude, short duration and polyphasic - which requires the patient to be awake and collaborative enough to perform voluntary contraction. Muscle necrosis in CIM is usually scattered rather than diffuse, so serum CK and myoglobin levels are typically normal and are not required for the diagnosis.
questions.topic: EMG diagnosis of critical illness myopathy

questions.question: Please classify as True/False about Tetanus:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Clinical features are caused by tetanospasmin, which stimulates substance P release

statements.label: B
statements.text: Onset may occur from 1 day to several months after the exposure

statements.label: C
statements.text: The shorter the time between exposure and first spasms, the more severe is the disease

statements.label: D
statements.text: Opisthotonus – severe intermittent decerebrate posturing – is a classical manifestation of tetanus

questions.explanation: Tetanospasmin impairs inhibitory synaptic vesicle release, rather than stimulating substance P release. Onset can range from one day to several months after exposure, and a shorter incubation period is associated with more severe disease. Opisthotonus - severe hyperextension and spasticity causing the head, neck and back to form an arch or 'bridging' posture - is a classical manifestation of tetanus.

questions.question: In tetanus:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Pain is rare because the nerve fibres are damaged by the toxin

statements.label: B
statements.text: Autonomic dysfunction, if present, excludes the diagnosis

statements.label: C
statements.text: Intrathecal administration of human tetanus immunoglobulin is a better therapeutic option than intravenous injection

statements.label: D
statements.text: Magnesium can help to stabilize the cardiovascular system

questions.explanation: Pain can be excruciating in tetanus, since muscle spasms are induced even by minor stimuli. Autonomic dysfunction - rapid fluctuations in heart rate and blood pressure, profuse sweating, and life-threatening tachy- or bradyarrhythmias or unexpected cardiac arrest - is frequently observed in severe tetanus rather than excluding the diagnosis. Intravenous (not intrathecal) immunoglobulin is the standard of care to neutralise the circulating toxin. Magnesium induces muscle relaxation and can help control both muscle spasms and cardiovascular instability.
questions.topic: clinical features and treatment of tetanus

questions.question: If a critical illness polyneuropathy (CIP) is suspected:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Muscle strength examination is required

statements.label: B
statements.text: Sensory testing is required

statements.label: C
statements.text: Neurological examination may reveal focal signs

statements.label: D
statements.text: Neurophysiological examination may reveal a sharp reduction of nerve conduction velocity

questions.explanation: CIP is a sensory-motor axonal polyneuropathy causing generalised, diffuse and symmetric muscle weakness involving all four limbs, so both muscle strength and sensory testing are required to characterise it. Nerve conduction velocity is normal or near-normal in CIP (a sharp reduction would suggest a demyelinating process instead), and focal neurological signs such as monoparesis or hemiparesis indicate a different cause of weakness, usually an acute brain disease.
questions.topic: clinical assessment of suspected critical illness polyneuropathy

questions.question: Please classify as True/False about Botulism:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Its toxin causes a demyelinating neuropathy

statements.label: B
statements.text: Symptoms occur 2-3 weeks after exposure

statements.label: C
statements.text: Motor signs are slightly worse than sensory signs

statements.label: D
statements.text: High fever is a common feature

questions.explanation: Botulinum toxin causes a neuromuscular blockade, not a demyelinating neuropathy; only motor nerve transmission is affected, with no sensory signs at all (so motor signs cannot meaningfully be compared with absent sensory signs). Symptoms usually occur 6 hours to 8 days after exposure, not 2-3 weeks, and high fever is not a typical feature of botulism.

questions.question: You are called to see a 30-year-old male ASA I patient in the operating theatre recovery area. He had a simple hernia repair under general anaesthesia and was extubated apparently uneventfully. After being transferred to the recovery room, he suddenly stops breathing, becomes cyanotic and needs to be re-intubated, with no respiratory effort observed. He is transferred to the ICU. Train-of-four stimulus testing performed in recovery was normal. He regains consciousness but not the ability to breathe spontaneously nor to move his limbs; sensation is intact. The ECG reveals infrequent ventricular ectopic beats and a ten-second episode of complete heart block. His mother, called in urgently, has a notably firm handshake, slurred speech, and wears thick-lensed 'pebble' glasses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: [CONSTRUCTED] Built from an ESICM course case-based self-assessment (interactive scenario, not a scored Final Assessment MCQ) rather than transcribed from a graded quiz item. A normal train-of-four excludes residual competitive neuromuscular blockade as the cause, and intact sensation argues against a primary sensory neuropathy. The combination of unexplained postoperative weakness, a cardiac conduction abnormality, and a parent with myotonic grip (difficulty relaxing a handshake), dysarthria and early cataracts ('pebble' glasses) is characteristic of myotonic dystrophy, an autosomal dominant multisystem disorder that is frequently first unmasked by an anaesthetic.
questions.topic: diagnosis of myotonic dystrophy after anaesthesia (case-based)

questions.question: A 30-year-old man fails to breathe spontaneously or move his limbs after tracheal extubation following an uncomplicated hernia repair; train-of-four testing is normal and sensation is intact. Regarding the differential diagnosis of his weakness, indicate whether each statement is TRUE or FALSE:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Surgical factors are a likely explanation, given that this was a lower abdominal procedure

statements.label: B
statements.text: Ongoing competitive neuromuscular blockade is the most likely explanation, given the normal train-of-four testing

statements.label: C
statements.text: If suxamethonium was used for induction, pseudocholinesterase deficiency causing an abnormally prolonged block should be considered

statements.label: D
statements.text: Pre-existing, previously undiagnosed neuromuscular disease should still be considered, even with no prior history

questions.explanation: [CONSTRUCTED] Built from an ESICM course case-based self-assessment rather than a scored Final Assessment item. In the context of a lower abdominal procedure it is unlikely that surgical factors play a role in ventilatory weakness (unlike major thoracic, gastric or oesophageal surgery, which can impair ventilation via diaphragmatic splinting/injury or phrenic nerve damage). A normal train-of-four argues against ongoing competitive neuromuscular blockade as the cause, but does not exclude an abnormally prolonged effect of a non-competitive agent such as suxamethonium in a patient with pseudocholinesterase deficiency. Pre-existing neuromuscular conditions - some muscular dystrophies, myasthenia gravis, neuropathies - although unlikely, may first present in this manner.

questions.question: A 30-year-old man with unexplained postoperative apnoea is now suspected of having myotonic dystrophy, an autosomal dominant disease, based on his clinical course and examination findings in a parent. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Refer to neurology and to a centre for genetic counselling
Reassure the family and discharge as soon as weaned
Start long-term home non-invasive ventilation without further investigation
questions.explanation: [CONSTRUCTED] Built from an ESICM course case-based self-assessment rather than a scored Final Assessment item. Myotonic dystrophy is a multisystem, autosomal dominant disorder with implications for the patient's cardiac and respiratory management as well as for relatives; once suspected, referral to neurology (for confirmation and ongoing management) and to a genetic counselling centre is the appropriate next step. There is no acute disease-modifying therapy such as corticosteroids or plasma exchange for myotonic dystrophy, and discharge without further workup would miss an important diagnosis with family implications.
questions.topic: management and referral after suspected myotonic dystrophy (case-based)

questions.question: A 43-year-old woman is treated by her family doctor with antibiotics for a mild upper respiratory tract infection. Two days later she develops diarrhoea, which resolves over four days. One week after that she notices cramp in her calves, then starts tripping over furniture. She is initially discharged from hospital with a diagnosis of 'hysteria', but returns the next day unable to get out of a chair and is admitted. She now complains of difficulty breathing; blood gases are normal, and she has no sensory signs. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: [CONSTRUCTED] Built from an ESICM course case-based self-assessment rather than a scored Final Assessment item. An acute, progressive, ascending weakness in a previously well person, following an antecedent infective illness and without sensory signs, is a classic presentation of Guillain-Barré syndrome; this acute presentation in someone previously well also precludes most other causes of weakness. A normal blood gas does not exclude significant respiratory compromise, since blood gases in acute neuromuscular weakness are typically normal until close to the point of respiratory arrest.

questions.question: A previously well 43-year-old woman develops progressive ascending limb weakness and breathlessness one week after a diarrhoeal illness, with no sensory signs; Guillain-Barré syndrome is suspected. Regarding monitoring of her respiratory function, indicate whether each statement is TRUE or FALSE:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Arterial blood gases are a reliable early warning sign of impending respiratory failure in this condition

statements.label: B
statements.text: Serial Forced Vital Capacity (FVC) measurement is the recommended way to monitor her respiratory status

statements.label: C
statements.text: An FVC below 1 L or below 20 mL/kg, or a rapidly declining FVC, should prompt consideration of mechanical ventilation

statements.label: D
statements.text: A Maximal Inspiratory Pressure (MIP) above 30 cmH2O predicts impending respiratory failure

questions.explanation: [CONSTRUCTED] Built from an ESICM course case-based self-assessment rather than a scored Final Assessment item. Blood gases in most patients with acute neuromuscular weakness remain normal until the time of respiratory arrest, so they are not a useful early warning sign; serial FVC is the recommended monitoring tool. An absolute FVC below 1 L or below 20 mL/kg, or an FVC that is rapidly declining on serial measurement, should prompt consideration of mechanical ventilation. A Maximal Inspiratory Pressure below (not above) 30 cmH2O, or a Maximal Expiratory Pressure below 40 cmH2O, are the values that predict impending acute respiratory failure. Any clinical suspicion of aspiration from coughing or swallowing difficulty should also prompt airway protection, usually by tracheal intubation initially.

questions.question: A 43-year-old woman with confirmed Guillain-Barré syndrome requires specific, disease-modifying treatment. Which of the following describes the appropriate treatment and how it is typically delivered?
options: Intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, the latter usually delivered via a dialysis catheter
Broad-spectrum antibiotics targeting the antecedent infection
Oral anticholinesterase therapy such as pyridostigmine
questions.explanation: [CONSTRUCTED] Built from an ESICM course case-based self-assessment rather than a scored Final Assessment item. The specific treatments for Guillain-Barré syndrome are intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, the latter usually delivered via a dialysis catheter; either therapy reduces time spent on mechanical ventilation and promotes faster recovery of mobility. Corticosteroids are not an effective treatment for Guillain-Barré syndrome (unlike some other neuromuscular conditions), and antibiotics, anticholinesterases and antitoxin are not disease-modifying here.

questions.question: A patient with Guillain-Barré syndrome has had a notably rapid onset and progression of weakness. Regarding prognosis and long-term outcome in Guillain-Barré syndrome, indicate whether each statement is TRUE or FALSE:

statements.label: A
statements.text: A rapid rate of symptom progression is generally associated with a better long-term physical recovery

statements.label: B
statements.text: Up to 20% of patients have long-term residual motor dysfunction and require ventilatory support early in their illness

statements.label: C
statements.text: Symptom onset is typically vague and progresses slowly, though rapid progression can occur

statements.label: D
statements.text: The rate of disease progression has no bearing on the ultimate degree of recovery

questions.explanation: [CONSTRUCTED] Built from an ESICM course case-based self-assessment rather than a scored Final Assessment item. Rapid progression of Guillain-Barré syndrome is usually associated with a poorer, not better, physical recovery. Although most patients make a good neurological recovery overall, up to 20% will have long-term residual motor dysfunction and will have required ventilatory support early in the course of their illness. Symptoms typically begin vaguely and progress slowly, which is part of why the diagnosis is often missed early, although rapid progression - as in a patient with a poorer prognosis - can also occur.

questions.question: A 68-year-old woman is admitted to the ICU after emergency surgery for a perforated colonic diverticulum with gross faecal peritoneal contamination; she develops septic shock requiring norepinephrine and renal dysfunction requiring continuous veno-venous haemofiltration. Two weeks later, sedation is reduced: she opens her eyes spontaneously but makes minimal respiratory effort, has no response to painful stimuli other than grimace, diminished reflexes and a normal plantar response. Regarding the differential diagnosis of her weakness, indicate whether each statement is TRUE or FALSE:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Excessive sedation due to accumulated fentanyl is a plausible explanation

statements.label: B
statements.text: Critical illness polyneuropathy (CIP) is a plausible explanation

statements.label: C
statements.text: Electrophysiological studies are mandatory in every case before CIP can be considered as a diagnosis

statements.label: D
statements.text: Her normal plantar response and the absence of focal sensory loss argue against an acute stroke as the cause

questions.explanation: [CONSTRUCTED] Built from an ESICM course case-based self-assessment rather than a scored Final Assessment item. In a patient with renal dysfunction who has received a prolonged fentanyl infusion, accumulated opioid is a plausible cause of reduced consciousness and respiratory effort, alongside critical illness polyneuropathy, a frequent complication of prolonged critical illness. Investigations are not always necessary in this context - clinical skills and a compatible context can make the diagnosis of CIP almost certain, with further investigation reserved for cases where weakness persists despite rehabilitation. A normal plantar response and no focal or sensory signs point away from an acute central (stroke) cause.
questions.topic: differential diagnosis of weakness after critical illness (case-based)

questions.question: A patient recovering from septic shock and acute kidney injury is diagnosed with critical illness polyneuropathy (CIP) after failing to wean from mechanical ventilation. What is the appropriate management approach?
options: Intravenous immunoglobulin as first-line specific therapy
High-dose corticosteroids to reduce nerve inflammation
Supportive care only: continued respiratory support until weaning criteria are met, thromboembolism prophylaxis, physical therapy and pain management
Immediate nerve biopsy to guide therapy
questions.explanation: [CONSTRUCTED] Built from an ESICM course case-based self-assessment rather than a scored Final Assessment item. There is no specific treatment for critical illness polyneuropathy. Supportive treatment includes continued respiratory support until respiratory muscle strength improves and weaning criteria are met, together with standard supportive care: maintenance of thromboembolism prophylaxis, physical therapy and management of pain. Immunoglobulin, corticosteroids and plasma exchange are treatments for other neuromuscular conditions, not CIP.

questions.question: A patient recovering from critical illness polyneuropathy has her tracheal tube urgently changed, using etomidate and suxamethonium, after it becomes obstructed. Two minutes later she suffers a cardiac arrest. What is the most probable explanation?
options: Hyperkalaemic arrest from an exaggerated release of potassium provoked by suxamethonium in denervated, CIP-affected muscle
questions.explanation: [CONSTRUCTED] Built from an ESICM course case-based self-assessment rather than a scored Final Assessment item. Muscles denervated by critical illness polyneuropathy develop upregulated extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors; suxamethonium administered in this setting can provoke an exaggerated release of potassium, leading to a dangerously high serum potassium and a hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest. Although rare, this is a recognised life-threatening complication, which is why non-depolarising neuromuscular blocking agents are generally better suited for use in the ICU.
questions.topic: suxamethonium-induced hyperkalaemic arrest in denervating disease (case-based)

questions.question: A patient who suffered a hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest related to suxamethonium and critical illness polyneuropathy remains weak three weeks later, greatly limiting her functional independence. Regarding prognosis after critical illness neuromuscular weakness, indicate whether each statement is TRUE or FALSE:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Critical illness myopathy (CIM) generally has a better prognosis than critical illness polyneuropathy (CIP)

statements.label: B
statements.text: The severity of muscle weakness correlates closely with the electrophysiological diagnosis

statements.label: C
statements.text: A muscle needle biopsy showing a thick-filament myopathy pattern is associated with a good prognosis

statements.label: D
statements.text: Once an initial electrophysiological diagnosis has been made, re-referral to neurology is not useful even if weakness persists

questions.explanation: [CONSTRUCTED] Built from an ESICM course case-based self-assessment rather than a scored Final Assessment item. The severity of muscle weakness is not well correlated with the electrophysiological diagnosis, but the rapidity and completeness of recovery are, and CIM has a better prognosis than CIP. A neurologist or clinical neurophysiologist can help precisely define the pathological diagnosis, and a needle muscle biopsy can also be useful at this stage, since some histologic features - such as a thick-filament myopathy pattern - are associated with a good prognosis. Electrophysiological investigations of peripheral nerves and muscle, and re-referral to neurology, remain useful if weakness persists despite rehabilitation.

questions.question: A young man is brought to the emergency department after being found acutely agitated and behaviourally disturbed. He shortly afterwards has a generalised convulsion. On assessment he remains unconscious, is hypertensive and pyrexial, and has reduced respiratory effort; he does not move his legs. He is intubated for airway protection and admitted to the ICU. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Drug-induced rhabdomyolysis, from a stimulant such as cocaine or amphetamines, possibly worsened by status-epilepticus-related muscle contraction
questions.explanation: [CONSTRUCTED] Built from an ESICM course case-based self-assessment; the opening vignette here has been reconstructed from the accompanying answer text, as the source slide stating the presenting scenario was not available (only the diagnostic reasoning and subsequent management slides were captured) - verify against the original ESICM material if possible. Initial behavioural disturbance followed by a convulsion, hypertension and pyrexia is suggestive of stimulant intoxication, with cocaine or amphetamines the likeliest agents; the resulting muscle damage is almost certainly drug-induced rhabdomyolysis, which may also occur due to, or be worsened by, status-epilepticus-induced agonist-antagonist muscle contraction.

questions.question: A young man develops severe rhabdomyolysis (creatine kinase greater than 100,000 U/L, serum potassium 5.9 mmol/L) following a convulsion and suspected stimulant intoxication. Regarding the pathophysiology and immediate consequences of his condition, indicate whether each statement is TRUE or FALSE:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Muscle contents leaking into the circulation can damage distant organs

statements.label: B
statements.text: A hyperacute rise in serum potassium is a recognised, immediately life-threatening consequence

statements.label: C
statements.text: The associated acute kidney injury is caused solely by direct nephrotoxicity of myoglobin, with hypovolaemia playing no role

statements.label: D
statements.text: An acid urine promotes myoglobin deposition in the renal tubules

questions.explanation: [CONSTRUCTED] Built from an ESICM course case-based self-assessment rather than a scored Final Assessment item. Clinical problems in rhabdomyolysis arise from muscle content leaking into the circulation and damaging distant organs, and from the metabolic consequences of the 'rhabdomyolysis syndrome', particularly a hyperacute rise in serum potassium. The associated oliguria is initially driven primarily by hypovolaemia, not myoglobin toxicity alone, and an acid urine promotes myoglobin deposition in the renal tubules - together these are recognised risk factors for acute kidney injury.

questions.question: In a patient with severe drug-induced rhabdomyolysis (creatine kinase greater than 100,000 U/L, serum potassium 5.9 mmol/L) whose toxic aetiology has been diagnosed and is being managed, what is the appropriate supportive management of the rhabdomyolysis itself?
options: Restrict intravenous fluids to limit compartment syndrome risk
Secure the airway, ensure adequate ventilation and oxygenation, control temperature and prevent further convulsions, together with aggressive fluid resuscitation
Give early urinary alkalinisation as the first priority, ahead of airway or circulatory management
Perform immediate prophylactic fasciotomy of all four limbs
Withhold intravenous fluids until creatine kinase has normalised
questions.explanation: [CONSTRUCTED] Built from an ESICM course case-based self-assessment rather than a scored Final Assessment item. The standard first priorities are to secure the airway, ensure adequate ventilation and oxygenation and, as in this patient, control temperature and prevent further convulsions. Fluid resuscitation is critical to circulatory management, since rhabdomyolysis induces oliguria (initially primarily due to hypovolaemia) and an acid urine, both of which are associated with myoglobin deposition in the renal tubules and are risks for acute kidney injury.

questions.question: A patient is recovering from severe rhabdomyolysis and is being monitored for ongoing muscle injury and its complications. Regarding muscle-focused monitoring in this setting, indicate whether each statement is TRUE or FALSE:

statements.label: A
statements.text: Creatine kinase should be expected to decline by about 50% per day, in the absence of ongoing muscle damage or renal dysfunction

statements.label: B
statements.text: Compartment syndrome is not a recognised complication and does not need to be monitored for

statements.label: C
statements.text: In the absence of haemoglobinuria, a positive 'blood' (haemoglobin) reaction on urine dipstick can serve as an indirect surrogate marker for myoglobinuria

statements.label: D
statements.text: Urine dipstick testing has no role whatsoever in monitoring rhabdomyolysis

questions.explanation: [CONSTRUCTED] Built from an ESICM course case-based self-assessment rather than a scored Final Assessment item. Creatine kinase should be monitored to gauge the amount of muscle damaged; its activity should decline at about 50% per day unless there is continuing muscle damage or renal dysfunction. Clinicians should remain aware that a compartment syndrome may develop and may need muscle- and limb-preserving intervention. Urine dipstick testing can be useful indirectly: presuming there is no haemoglobinuria, the 'haemoglobin' reaction on the dipstick can be used as a surrogate marker for myoglobin.
